newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Clinton in lightning visit to encourage Romanians.
newsitem.headline: Clinton in lightning visit to encourage Romanians.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived for a lightning visit to Romania on Friday to encourage the Balkan country to pursue reforms and persist with its bid for NATO membership.

Clinton, the first U.S. president to visit Romania in 22 years, arrived from Warsaw, one of three ex-communist countries invited to join the Western alliance this week along with Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The centre piece of his eight-hour stop will be an address in a central square, where the president is expected to tell Romanians not to be discouraged by the decision to leave their country out of NATO's initial eastward expansion.

Still recovering from a knee injury earlier this year, he stepped gingerly down the ramp from Air Force One to be greeted by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, the driving force behind Romania's late-starting market reforms.

He was then whisked straight off to the Cotroceni Palace for talks with President Emil Constantinescu, whose election along with a centrist parliament last year ended seven years of rule by ex-communists.
Hundreds of Bucharest residents, many carrying small stars-and-stripes flags lined roads leading from Otopeni airport. Main thoroughfares were blocked off 24 hours in advance of Clinton's arrival.

Although opinion polls show Romanians overwhelmingly support NATO membership, Romania's leaders have accepted the Madrid decision gracefully with expressions of determination to carry on with reform programmes first launched in February.
In addition to aspiring to Alliance membership, Romanian officials want a "strategic partnership" with Washington.

Clinton's Deputy National Security Adviser, James Steinberg, told reporters aboard Air Force One that Romania was on the right track. But it had to prove reforms were durable for the next review of enlargement, due in 1999.
"We believe generally they are on the right track across the board. one of the main reasons that we think they aren't ready yet is that this is a new process and needs to be deepened," he said.

"We have a lot of respect for what they've done. And we want to let them know that if they stay on the course, the prospects of integration into Western institutions, including NATO, remain a real possibility."

Officials said Clinton wanted to stress that the United States was open to adding additional members to NATO and that Romania, along with Slovenia, would be a leading contender if it continued on its road of reform.
Clinton told a large crowd in Warsaw's Castle Square, Clinton on Thursday welcomed Poland's acceptance into NATO as a chance to create a new Europe through "the power of peace."
In a toast at the presidential palace, he said the initial wave of expansion meant "the old dividing lines of Europe were wiped away forever."
Romania's break with communism was more dramatic and bloody than those in any of the three successful NATO entrants.
More than 1,500 people were killed in the 1989 uprising that overthrew Nicolae Ceausescu, whose 24-year rule grew into one of eastern Europe's harshest Communist regimes.
Clinton was due to address Romanians in University Square, where dozens of students were killed in the upheaval.

In his early rule, Ceausescu was lionised by the United States for bucking Soviet-dictated policy. Two U.S. leaders visited Bucharest -- Richard Nixon in 1969 and his successor Gerald Ford six years later.

At the height of the Cold War, Romania was the sole east European country to have ties with West Germany in 1967 and refused to obey Moscow's injunction to sever ties with Israel after the Six Day War. Romania also rejected Moscow's orders to send troops to quell Czechoslovakia's 1968 "Prague Spring".
